title: Dazzling diamonds of Trumpler 14
caption: The star cluster Trumpler 14, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Trumpler 14 · constellation Carina · about 8000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA & ESA, Jesús Maíz Apellániz (Centro de Astrobiología, CSIC-INTA, Spain)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: A prominent dark patch sits close to the center of this Hubble view of the star cluster Trumpler 14. It is a Bok globule, a small, isolated dark nebula containing dense dust and gas, seen against the stars around it.

Few places in the Milky Way gather as many hot, massive, bright stars as Trumpler 14, and it contains several of the most luminous stars found anywhere in our galaxy. Massive stars are short-lived and pour out intense light, which makes clusters like this natural places to study stellar heavyweights.

Bok globules remain a subject of active research, because their internal structure and density are still something of a mystery. Dark nebulae like this one are visible only because they block the light of stars or glowing gas behind them, so they appear as shadows rather than shining objects.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.25 x 3.25 arcminutes) and distance (8000 light years), the frame spans roughly 7.6 × 7.6 light-years. Its light set out about 8,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using blue, visible, red and near-infrared filters. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the dark globule is seen only because it blocks light from behind it.
